periods.detail:
The Celts in Britain were Iron Age farming tribes and fierce warriors living in roundhouses before Roman rule.

periods.title: Roman Britain
periods.text: Rome governs Britain for four centuries.
periods.detail: For nearly four centuries, Rome governed Britain, constructing cities, paved roads, and defensive borders like Hadrian's Wall.

periods.title: Early Medieval Period

periods.detail: Norman rule, the Magna Carta, the Black Death, the Hundred Years’ War, and the Wars of the Roses.

events.title: Rome governs Britain
events.detail: For nearly four centuries, Rome governed Britain, constructing cities, paved roads, and defensive borders like Hadrian's Wall.

events.title: Invasion of Germanic tribes
events.detail: 5th century: Invasion of Germanic tribes (Angles, Saxons, Jutes) from Continental Europe to England.

events.title: St Augustine's mission
events.detail: Christianity is on the rise in Britain in the 6th century. St. Augustine leads a mission to the pagan Anglo-Saxons and converts King Æthelberht.

events.title: Viking raids begin (Lindisfarne)
events.detail: Vikings started raiding coastal monasteries in the 8th century. In the 9th century they conquered parts of England and established the Danelaw.

events.title: Danelaw established
events.detail: Vikings started raiding coastal monasteries in the 8th century. In the 9th century they conquered parts of England and established the Danelaw.

events.title: England unified (Alfred the Great)
events.detail: Late 9th century: England is unified under king Alfred the Great. He defends England against the Viking raids and conquest.

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.detail: Norman Period: William the Conqueror wins the fight for England at the Battle of Hastings (1066). His dynasty rules England until the Plantagenets take over in 1154.

events.title: Domesday Book
events.detail: Domesday Book (1086): a detailed record of a survey of England. It lists who owned what land, how much the property was worth, and how much tax people owed.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.detail: The Magna Carta (1215): A royal document signed by King John of England in 1215. One of the most famous documents in world history because it established the principle that everyone is subject to the law. English noblemen (barons) rebelled against the King due to his heavy taxes, failed wars, and abuse of power. The charter was a peace treaty to stop the civil war. The document established The Rule of Law: The king could no longer rule arbitrarily (he had to follow the law), no free man could be imprisoned or stripped of his property without a fair trial, and no unfair taxes (the king could not demand taxes without the common consent of the kingdom).

events.title: Black Death arrives
events.detail: Black Death (1348) arrives in England.

events.title: Hundred Years' War
events.text: England and France fight over the French throne.
events.detail: The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) was a long conflict between England and France over who should rule the French throne. England dominated early on at famous battles like Agincourt. However, France launched a dramatic comeback inspired by Joan of Arc and eventually drove the English out. The war transformed both countries from fractured medieval kingdoms into unified, modern nations.

events.title: Wars of the Roses
events.detail: The Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) were bloody civil wars between two rival royal families: House of Lancaster (red rose) and House of York (white rose). Triggered by a weak king and greed for the throne, bringing decades of chaos. The wars ended when Henry Tudor defeated Richard III.

events.title: Act of Supremacy
events.text: Henry VIII heads the Church of England.
events.detail: The Act of Supremacy (1534) declared King Henry VIII the Head of the Church of England, permanently breaking ties with the Pope and marking the official birth of the Anglican Church.

events.title: Union of Wales & England
events.text: Welsh citizens gain equal legal status.
events.detail: Union of Wales & England (1536) provided Welsh citizens equal legal status, it also established English as the sole language of government, suppressing official use of the Welsh language.

events.title: Spanish Armada defeated
events.detail: The English navy decisively defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588, thwarting Spain's invasion attempt.

events.title: Union of the Crowns
events.text: James VI inherits the English throne.
events.detail: The Union of the Crowns (1603) happened when King James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne, bringing both realms under the rule of one king. However, the regions only shared a king, they remained separate countries.

events.title: English Civil War
events.detail: The English Civil War reached its climax in 1649 when Parliament executed King Charles I, abolished the monarchy, and declared England a republic known as the Commonwealth. Oliver Cromwell then seized control, using the New Model Army to crush royalist uprisings in Scotland and Ireland while establishing a strict Puritan military dictatorship. This permanently shattered the idea of the divine right of kings.

events.title: Glorious Revolution
events.detail: The Glorious Revolution (1688) was the largely peaceful overthrow of the Catholic King James II, who was replaced by his Protestant daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband, William of Orange. William and Mary signed the Bill of Rights, permanently limiting royal power.

events.title: Acts of Union (Scotland)
events.detail: The Acts of Union (1707) permanently joined England and Scotland into a single, unified nation (Kingdom of Great Britain) merging their two parliaments into one centralized government in London.

events.title: US Independence
events.detail: US independence: Frustrated by British taxes without representation, American colonists rebelled, sparked the Revolutionary War, and declared independence on July 4, 1776, creating a new sovereign nation. Great Britain officially recognized the United States as an independent nation on September 3, 1783.

events.title: Act of Union with Ireland
events.detail: After the Irish Rebellion of 1798, the British forced through the Acts of Union (1801), legally merging Great Britain and Ireland into a single state: the United Kingdom.

events.title: Industrial Revolution & Empire
events.detail: During the Victorian era, steam-powered industrialization peaked, making Britain the world's workshop and fueling the expansion of history's largest global empire. This massive empire ruled one-quarter of the globe, encompassing vital territories like India, Canada, and Australia.

events.title: World War I
events.detail: The World Wars devastated Britain financially, accelerating the collapse of its empire. Despite victories in 1918 and 1945, severe postwar debt and surging global nationalism forced Britain to decolonize.

events.title: Irish Free State
events.detail: Following the 1916 rebellion and war, Ireland achieved freedom from England, creating the Irish Free State (1922).

events.title: World War II
events.detail: The World Wars devastated Britain financially, accelerating the collapse of its empire. Despite victories in 1918 and 1945, severe postwar debt and surging global nationalism forced Britain to decolonize.

events.title: Decolonization
events.text: India, Ghana, Kenya and others gain independence.
events.detail: Decolonization: Following India's independence in 1947, Britain rapidly decolonized across Africa and Asia, withdrawing from nations like Ghana (1957) and Kenya (1963). This dissolved the empire and shrunk British global influence.

dynasties.title: House of Wessex (Alfred the Great)
dynasties.detail: Alfred the Great was the first to propose a unified England for the Anglo-Saxon people.

dynasties.title: Norman dynasty
dynasties.detail: William the Conqueror, a Norman duke from France, ruled England alongside his French-speaking nobility. During this period, French became the language of the elite, heavily influencing the development of English.

dynasties.title: The Plantagenets
dynasties.text: Henry II, Richard the Lionheart, Henry V.
dynasties.detail: The Plantagenet dynasty (1154–1485) shaped medieval England by transforming its law, architecture, and language through exceptionally powerful and ambitious rulers. The dynasty consisted of kings like Henry II, who established English Common Law and the jury system, Richard the Lionheart, the legendary Crusader knight, and Henry V, the brilliant warrior who conquered France at the Battle of Agincourt. Under Plantagenet rule, England built magnificent Gothic cathedrals and established early representative Parliaments.

dynasties.title: The Tudors
dynasties.detail: The Tudors (1485-1603): A vibrant era shaped by powerful monarchs like Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. This period brought the English Reformation, the birth of the Church of England, and immense cultural growth, ending permanently when Elizabeth died without an heir.

dynasties.title: The Stuarts
dynasties.detail: The Stuarts (1603-1649): James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, uniting the crowns. This era was defined by deep religious tension and ongoing power struggles between the king and Parliament over taxation and royal authority.

dynasties.title: Commonwealth
dynasties.detail: Commonwealth (1649-1660): The king was executed at the end of the civil war and England became a republic (the Commonwealth). Oliver Cromwell emerged as the military dictator and Lord Protector.

dynasties.title: Restoration (Stuarts return)
dynasties.detail: (Restoration, 1660-1714): The Stuarts returned. Charles II was invited back from exile to reclaim the throne, restoring the traditional monarchy and reopening theaters.

dynasties.title: Georgian period (Hanover)
dynasties.detail: Georgian period (1714-1837): The Hanoverian dynasty ruled Britain through four Georges and William IV, shifting power from the monarchy to parliament before Victoria's accession. The period is famous for the American Revolutionary War and the Napoleonic Wars.

dynasties.title: Victorian period
dynasties.detail: The Victorian period (1837-1901) was defined by Queen Victoria's 63-year reign, which reshaped the monarchy from a politically dominant force into a symbolic institution.

dynasties.title: Edwardian
dynasties.detail: The Edwardian era (1901-1910) was a brief but golden age of optimism, modernization and luxury under King Edward VII.

dynasties.title: House of Windsor / Modern Britain
dynasties.detail: Modern Britain: Since 1910, the House of Windsor has stabilized the British monarchy through two World Wars and immense social change. Shifting from imperial rulers to ceremonial figureheads, they survived crises like the 1936 abdication and celebrated Queen Elizabeth II’s historic reign.

literary.title: Anglo-Saxon / Old English
literary.detail: The Anglo-Saxon literary period flourished in oral warrior epics like Beowulf. Written in Old-English and combining heroic tribalism and fate with Christian themes.

literary.title: Middle English
literary.text: Chaucer, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
literary.detail: The Middle English period is marked by two iconic texts, both written at the end of the 14th century. The Canterbury Tales, written by Geoffrey Chaucer, the "Father of English literature." His story uses a framing narrative of twenty-nine pilgrims traveling to Canterbury to deliver a sharp, satirical, and human cross-section of society. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, written by an anonymous poet, is a chivalric romance that tests the honor and purity of King Arthur’s nephew against a magical foe, balancing the period’s love for French courtly ideals with native English folklore.

literary.title: Renaissance
literary.detail: A period of cultural and literary rebirth (1500-1660) influenced by European humanism, classical Greek and Roman texts, and new scientific ideas. Writers shifted from medieval religious focus to human potential, individualism, and secular themes. Drama reached its peak through the blank-verse tragedies of William Shakespeare and Christopher Marlowe, while poetry thrived with the introduction of the Elizabethan sonnet, Edmund Spenser's grand epic allegories, and John Donne's intellectual Metaphysical poetry.

literary.title: Restoration literature
literary.detail: Restoration literature, led by John Dryden, is characterized by its witty comedy, biting satire, and a shift toward reason.

literary.title: Neoclassical
literary.text: Pope and Swift: reason and wit.
literary.detail: Writers like Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift emphasized reason, order and wit.

literary.title: Romanticism
literary.detail:
Writers like Wordsworth emphasized emotion, sublime nature, imagination & individualism.

literary.title: Victorian literature
literary.detail: Victorian writers explored morality, class anxiety, imperialism, and science vs faith. Famous names include Charles Dickens and the Brontë sisters.

literary.title: Modernism
literary.detail: Writers like Virginia Woolf, James Joyce and T.S. Eliot rejected traditional forms, exploring psychology, stream of consciousness, and post-war disillusionment.

literary.title: Postmodernism
literary.detail: Postmodernism embraced fragmentation, irony, skepticism, and playful subversion of traditional storytelling.
